ican: I can state Newton's third law and name the reaction force.
I can explain how a rocket launches, using Newton's third law.
I can calculate the unbalanced force, then the acceleration with F = ma.
I can show and name the forces on a rocket.
I can explain why a rocket's acceleration changes.

cloze.title: Say it the exam way
cloze.text:
At launch, the rocket pushes the exhaust gases [[down|up]]. The exhaust gases push the rocket [[up|down]]. This is Newton's [[third|first]] law.

On a force diagram, the upward force is the [[engine thrust|upthrust]] and the downward force is the [[weight|gravity]]. The unbalanced force is thrust [[minus|plus]] weight.

As fuel is used, the mass [[decreases|increases]]. The weight falls, so the unbalanced force [[increases|decreases]] and the acceleration [[increases|decreases]].

mc.alt: During a rocket launch, the thrust of the rocket engine remains constant. A student makes three statements about the motion of the rocket during its launch. I: the acceleration of the rocket increases because the mass of the rocket decreases as fuel is used up. II: the acceleration of the rocket increases because the unbalanced force acting on the rocket increases. III: the rocket moves upwards because the exhaust gases exert a downward force on the Earth. Which of these statements is or are correct? A I only, B II only, C III only, D I and II only, E I, II and III.
fb: Not this one. I is right, but II is right too. As the mass falls, the weight falls, so the unbalanced force (thrust − weight) increases.
Not this one. II is right, but so is I. Less mass means more acceleration for the same force (<var>a</var> = <var>F</var> ÷ <var>m</var>).
Not this one. III is wrong. The exhaust gases push the rocket up. The force pair is the rocket and the gases, not the gases and the Earth.
Right. I and II are both true: the mass decreases and the unbalanced force increases, so the acceleration increases. III is wrong: the gases push the rocket up (Newton's third law).
Not this one. III is wrong. The rocket is pushed up by the exhaust gases, not by the gases pushing on the Earth.

mc.alt: A student is investigating the motion of water rockets. A drawing shows a water rocket standing on the ground, with pressurised air above the water and a tube to an air pump. Air is pumped into the rocket until the pressure of the air inside is large enough for the water rocket to launch upwards. The rocket launches because: A the rocket pushes down on the ground and the ground provides a reaction force pushing up on the rocket, B the rocket pushes down on the water and the water provides a reaction force pushing up on the rocket, C the water pushes down on the ground and the ground provides a reaction force pushing up on the water, D the force applied by the water on the ground is greater than the weight of the rocket producing an unbalanced upward force, E the weight of the rocket decreases as water is pushed out of the rocket producing an unbalanced upward force.
fb: Not this one. Once the rocket leaves the ground there is no ground force. The pair is between the rocket and the water.
Right. Newton's third law: the rocket pushes the water down, and the water pushes the rocket up.
Not this one. This pair acts on the water and the ground, not on the rocket.
Not this one. The water does not need to push on the ground. The rocket is pushed by the water it throws out.
Not this one. Losing water does reduce the weight, but that is not what makes the rocket launch. Look for the force pair.

mc.alt: A spacecraft has four rocket engines P, Q, R and S and is travelling to the right. P and Q are at the back (left) end and point backwards; R and S are at the front (right) end and point forwards. When switched on, each rocket engine produces the same amount of force. Which rocket engines are switched on to reduce the speed of the spacecraft? A R and S, B Q and S, C P and Q, D P and R, E P, Q, R and S.
fb: Right. R and S push gas forwards (to the right). The gas pushes the spacecraft back (to the left), against its motion, so it slows down.
Not this one. Q pushes the spacecraft forwards and S pushes it backwards. The forces cancel.
Not this one. P and Q push gas backwards, so the gas pushes the spacecraft forwards. It speeds up.
Not this one. P and R push in opposite directions. The forces cancel.
Not this one. All four push equally in opposite directions. The forces are balanced, so the speed does not change.

mc.alt: A rocket accelerates vertically upwards from the surface of the Earth. An identical rocket accelerates vertically upwards from the surface of Mars. The engine thrust from each rocket is the same. Which row in the table shows how the weight of the rocket and the unbalanced force acting on the rocket compare on Mars and Earth? Weight on Mars compared to weight on Earth, then unbalanced force on Mars compared to unbalanced force on Earth: A greater, greater. B same, same. C same, less. D less, greater. E less, less.
fb: Not this one. <var>g</var> on Mars (3.7 N kg<sup>−1</sup>) is less than on Earth (9.8 N kg<sup>−1</sup>), so the weight on Mars is less.
Not this one. Weight is <var>W</var> = <var>mg</var>, and <var>g</var> is different on Mars.
Not this one. Same mass, but <var>g</var> is smaller on Mars, so the weight is less.
Right. W = mg and g is smaller on Mars, so the weight is less. Unbalanced force = thrust − weight. Same thrust, less weight, so the unbalanced force is greater.
Not this one. The weight is less, but work out thrust − weight. A smaller weight leaves a greater unbalanced force.

mc.alt: A spacecraft completes the last stage of its journey back to Earth by parachute, falling with constant speed into the sea. The spacecraft falls with constant speed because: A the gravitational field strength of the Earth is constant near the Earth's surface, B it has come from space where the gravitational field strength is almost zero, C the air resistance is greater than the weight of the spacecraft, D the weight of the spacecraft is greater than the air resistance, E the air resistance is equal to the weight of the spacecraft.
fb: Not this one. True, but a constant <var>g</var> does not explain a constant speed. A constant speed needs balanced forces.
Not this one. Where it came from does not matter. Look at the forces acting on it now.
Not this one. If air resistance were bigger than the weight, the unbalanced force would be upwards and the spacecraft would slow down.
Not this one. Then the unbalanced force is downwards and the spacecraft speeds up.
Right. The forces are balanced, so the speed stays constant (Newton's first law).

p2_tip: Write the relationship first, every time. For an acceleration, find the unbalanced force first: thrust − weight. Values of <var>g</var> are on the data sheet given in each exam paper.

paper2.alt: The Falcon Heavy rocket is used to carry a satellite from Earth into space. (a)(i) The total mass of the rocket and satellite at launch is 1.43 times 10 to the 6 kilograms. Calculate the weight of the rocket and satellite at launch. 3 marks.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for 2025 Question 2(a)(i). W = mg (1). W = 1.43 times 10 to the 6, times 9.8 (1). W = 1.4 times 10 to the 7 newtons (1). Accept 1 times 10 to the 7, 1.40 times 10 to the 7, 1.401 times 10 to the 7.

paper2.alt: NASA is planning a crewed mission to the Moon. (a) Part of the mission includes placing a spacecraft in orbit at an altitude of 140 km above the surface of the Moon. A graph shows the gravitational field strength at different altitudes above the surface of the Moon: a straight line falling from 1.6 newtons per kilogram at 0 km to about 1.1 newtons per kilogram at 400 km. One of the astronauts selected for the mission has a mass of 67 kg. Calculate the weight of this astronaut when they are at an altitude of 140 km above the surface of the Moon. 3 marks. (c) After spending time on the Moon, the astronauts will return to the orbiting spacecraft using the transportation module. During the first part of this return journey, the rockets on the transportation module will exert a constant upward force. State what will happen to the acceleration of the transportation module during this part of the journey. You must justify your answer. 3 marks.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for 2024 Question 4. (a) W = mg (1), W = 67 times 1.4 (1), W = 94 N (1); accept 90, 93.8, 93.80. (c) Acceleration increases (1); 3 marks, must justify. Justification: mass decreases (as fuel is used) or gravitational field strength decreases (with altitude) (1); weight decreases or unbalanced force increases (1). Ignore any reference to air resistance or friction.

paper2.alt: A satellite is transported into space using a rocket. (b) The total mass of the rocket and satellite at launch is 5.5 times 10 to the 5 kilograms. (i) Show that the weight of the rocket and satellite at launch is 5.4 times 10 to the 6 newtons. 2 marks. (ii) The initial acceleration of the rocket and satellite at launch is 4.1 metres per second squared. Determine the initial upward thrust acting on the rocket. 4 marks.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for 2026 Question 4(b)(ii). F = ma (1). F = 5.5 times 10 to the 5, times 4.1 (1). Th minus W = F (1): Th minus 5.4 times 10 to the 6 = 5.5 times 10 to the 5 times 4.1 (1). Th = 7.7 times 10 to the 6 N (1). Accept 8 times 10 to the 6, 7.66 times 10 to the 6, 7.655 times 10 to the 6.

paper2.lead: Part (b)(i) is done in class. Use its answer: the weight is 5.4 × 10<sup>6</sup> N.

paper2.alt: In 2023, a spacecraft was launched from Earth to investigate the asteroid Psyche. Psyche is located in the asteroid belt, between Mars and Jupiter. The spacecraft will reach Psyche in 2029. A picture shows the spacecraft with two large solar panels. (b) On its journey, the spacecraft uses an ion drive engine to provide thrust. The ion drive engine produces a small unbalanced force on the spacecraft. (i) Explain how this small unbalanced force can still result in a large increase in speed, even though the spacecraft has a large mass. 1 mark.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for 2025 Question 4(b)(i). 1 mark: (the unbalanced force) is applied over an extended or long period of time.

paper2.alt: A spaceship on Mars is being prepared for the return journey to Earth. A photograph shows a rocket standing on the surface of Mars. (a) The mass of the spaceship including fuel and crew is 1.3 times 10 to the 6 kilograms. The rocket engines on the spaceship produce a constant upward thrust of 1.2 times 10 to the 7 newtons. (i) Calculate the weight of the spaceship on Mars. 3 marks. (ii) On the diagram below, show all the forces acting vertically on the spaceship just after it leaves the surface. You must name these forces and show their directions. 2 marks. A drawing of the rocket follows. (iii) Determine the acceleration of the spaceship at launch. 4 marks. (b) State what happens to the acceleration of the spaceship as its altitude increases. Justify your answer. 2 marks.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for 2022 Question 3. (a)(i) W = mg (1), W = 1.3 times 10 to the 6, times 3.7 (1), W = 4.8 times 10 to the 6 N (1). (a)(ii) An arrow up labelled engine thrust (1) and an arrow down labelled weight (1). Accept rocket thrust, force from exhaust gases on rocket, force due to gravity, gravitational pull, pull of gravity. Do not accept upward force alone, gravitational field strength alone, gravity alone, or upthrust. (a)(iii) Unbalanced force = engine thrust minus weight = 1.2 times 10 to the 7 minus 4.8 times 10 to the 6 (1), which is 7.2 times 10 to the 6 N. F = ma (1). 7.2 times 10 to the 6 = 1.3 times 10 to the 6 times a (1). a = 5.5 metres per second squared (1). (b) Acceleration increases (1). Weight or mass decreases (as fuel is used), or gravitational field strength decreases (1).

paper2.lead: <var>g</var> on Mars is on the data sheet given in each exam paper: 3.7 N kg<sup>−1</sup>.

paper2.alt: The Soyuz Spacecraft is used to transport astronauts from the International Space Station (ISS) to Earth. The spacecraft consists of three parts, shown in a drawing and a table: Orbital Module 1300 kg; Descent Module (including astronauts) 2950 kg; Instrumentation/Propulsion Module 2900 kg. (a) When the spacecraft leaves the ISS, the three parts are launched together. The propulsion module produces a force of 1430 N. Determine the acceleration of the spacecraft as it leaves the ISS. 4 marks.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for specimen Question 2(a). m = 1300 + 2950 + 2900 (1). F = ma (1). 1430 = (1300 + 2950 + 2900) times a (1). a = 0.200 metres per second squared (1). Accept 0.20, 0.2000, 0.20000; also accept 0.2.

paper2.alt: A water rocket consists of a plastic bottle partly filled with water. Air is pumped in through the water. When the pressure is great enough, the tube detaches from the bottle. Water is forced out of the bottle, which causes the bottle to be launched upwards. A drawing shows the bottle, pressurised air, water, a tube and a bicycle pump. At launch, the air in the bottle is at a pressure of 1.74 times 10 to the 5 pascals. (a) On the diagram below, show all the forces acting vertically on the bottle as it is launched. You must name these forces and show their directions. 2 marks. A drawing of the upturned bottle follows.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for 2019 Question 8(a). Independent marks; name and direction required for each mark. An arrow up labelled thrust (1) and an arrow down labelled weight or force of gravity (1). Accept force of water on air in bottle, force of water on rocket, gravitational pull, pull of gravity. Do not accept upward force alone, lift (force), upthrust, or gravity alone. Apply the plus or minus rule for surplus incorrect forces.

paper2.alt: On 12th November 2014, on a mission known as Rosetta, the European Space Agency successfully landed a probe on the surface of a comet. A drawing shows the spacecraft's main structure and solar arrays. The main structure of the Rosetta spacecraft consists of an orbiter, a lander and propellant. Rosetta spacecraft data: launch mass orbiter 1.23 times 10 cubed kg, lander 0.10 times 10 cubed kg, propellant 1.67 times 10 cubed kg, total 3.00 times 10 cubed kg; solar array output 850 W at 3.4 AU and 395 W at 5.25 AU; trajectory control 24 thrusters, 10 N of force each. (a) Calculate the total weight of the spacecraft on Earth. 3 marks. (c) At a point on its journey between Earth and the comet, the spacecraft was travelling at a constant velocity. (i) The spacecraft switched on four of its thrusters to accelerate it in the direction of travel. The four thrusters exerted a force on the spacecraft in the same direction. Determine the total force produced by these thrusters. 1 mark. (ii) At this point, the spacecraft had used 1.00 times 10 cubed kg of propellant. Calculate the acceleration of the spacecraft. 4 marks.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for 2016 Question 12. (a) W = mg (1), W = 3.00 times 10 cubed times 9.8 (1), W = 2.9 times 10 to the 4 N (1). (c)(i) 4 times 10 = 40 N (1); unit must be stated. (c)(ii) m = 3.00 times 10 cubed minus 1.00 times 10 cubed = 2.00 times 10 cubed kg (1). a = F over m (1). a = 40 over 2.00 times 10 cubed (1). a = 0.02 metres per second squared (1).

paper2.lead: Part (b) is about solar cells, so it is left out.

paper2.alt: A student is investigating the motion of water rockets. The water rocket is made from an upturned plastic bottle containing some water. Air is pumped into the bottle. When the pressure of the air is great enough the plastic bottle is launched upwards. A drawing shows the water rocket resting on its fins on the ground. The mass of the rocket before launch is 0.94 kg. (a) Calculate the weight of the water rocket. 3 marks. (d) At launch, the initial upward thrust on the rocket is 370 N. Calculate the initial acceleration of the rocket. 4 marks. (e) The student launches the rocket a second time. For this launch, the student adds a greater volume of water than before. The same initial upward thrust acts on the rocket but it fails to reach the same height. Explain why the rocket fails to reach the same height. 2 marks.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for 2014 Question 12. (a) W = mg (1), = 0.94 times 9.8 (1), = 9.2 N (1). (d) Unbalanced force = upthrust minus weight = 370 minus 9.2 = 360.8 N (1). a = F over m (1). = 360.8 over 0.94 (1). = 380 metres per second squared (1). (e) Any two from three: more water will increase weight or mass (1); unbalanced force decreases (1); acceleration is less (1).

paper2.lead: Parts (b) and (c) are not on this page.
